newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW - Zeneca "in touch with" pft targets.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Zeneca "in touch with" pft targets.

text.p: Zeneca Group Plc chief executive David Barnes said on Tuesday that 1996 results showed the company was "in touch with" his ambitious target of doubling profits by the end of the century.

Last year Barnes set what he called "an inspirational target" of increasing earnings per share (eps) by an average of 15 percent between 1996 and 2000. Before exceptional items, eps rose 14 percent last year to 70.6 pence, and after exceptionals jumped by 90 percent to 67.8 pence.
"The profit growth shows that we are in touch with that aspirational target," Barnes told Reuters in an interview .

He added that using 1992, the year before Zeneca's demerger from Imperial Chemical Industries Plc as a base, "profits are up 23 percent at a compound rate (year-on-year) and the 15 percent target continues to be someting we have a reasonable prospect of achieving."

Despite raising capital expenditure by 34 percent to 379 million stg last year and spending more than 600 million stg on research and development, Zeneca ended the year debt free. Barnes said the company would look at suitable acquisition and licensing opportunites if they came along.

"We are very alive to new product opportunities. We are alive to regional infill opportunities if they were to strengthen our business. If a good opportunity were to present itself by way of acquisition we would look at it, but here is no strategic imperative to do that. We have got strong organic growth," Barnes said.
He said one strategic move expected in 1997 would be the acquisiton of the remaining 50 percent of Salick, the U.S. cancer care company, which would cost around $240 million.
Barnes said sales of Zeneca's top-selling treatment, heart drug Zestril, grew by 10 percent last year, faster than the cardiovascular market as a whole.

Zestril loses its patent protection in 2001, but Barnes said new drugs such as Accolate for asthma, Zomig for migraine and Casodex for prostate cancer, as well as the agricultural fungicide Amistar, "should be significant products by the time we come to 2001."

Zeneca announced earlier on Tuesday that Zomig, acquired last year from Glaxo Wellcome Plc, had been approved in Britain on Monday. He said it would be "more than competitive" with the market leader, Glaxo Wellcome's Imigran.
Imigran sales soared to 539 million stg last year, and Glaxo Wellcome announced the first marketing approval of its own successor to Imigran, Naramig, earlier on Tuesday.

"It is a substantial market area and growing strongly," said Barnes, who who added that Zomig will go on sale in Britain "in the next few weeks." The drug is awaiting approval from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration.

Barnes said that "in the next 18 months profit growth in percentage terms will lag behind sales growth" because of costs linked to new product launches. He expects pharmaceutical profit margins to remain at around 30 percent this year.

"The key thing is that we have invested fully for the medium- to long-term with the launch of these new products, whether it be Amistar, Accolate or Zomig. That has some short-term costs but will increase margins in the long term," he said.
Barnes declined to be drawn on what would happen after his own contract as chief executive expires in 15 months time. Analysts expect the hunt for a successor to begin soon.
"The contract has 15 months to run. The board is aware of that and at an appropriate time they will announce what follows," he said.
